questions.question_text:
A line passes through $(1,-2)$ and $(5,4)$.
Find its angle of inclination, correct to the nearest degree.

options.why: Swapped rise and run, using $\tfrac{5-1}{4-(-2)}$ for the gradient.
Subtracted the coordinates in opposite orders, giving a gradient of $-1.5$.

questions.question_text:
A line passes through $(-2,3)$ and $(1,-3)$.
Find its angle of inclination, correct to the nearest degree.

options.why: Took the acute angle, ignoring that the negative gradient makes $\theta$ obtuse.
Used the raw $\tan^{-1}$ value without adding $180^{\circ}$.
Swapped rise and run, getting a gradient of $-0.5$.

questions.solution_text:
$m=\dfrac{-3-3}{1-(-2)}$
$=\dfrac{-6}{3}$
$=-2$
$\tan\theta=-2$
The calculator returns a negative angle. Add $180^{\circ}$ before rounding:
$\theta=\tan^{-1}(-2)+180^{\circ}$
$\approx117^{\circ}$

questions.question_text: Find the angle of inclination of the line $2x+3y=6$, correct to the nearest degree.

options.why: Used the acute angle for $m=\tfrac{2}{3}$, ignoring the negative gradient.
Did not add $180^{\circ}$ to the negative calculator value.
Reversed the ratio and dropped the negative sign, using $\tfrac{3}{2}$ instead of $-\tfrac{2}{3}$ before taking $\tan^{-1}$ and rounding to the nearest degree.

questions.solution_text:
Rearrange: $3y=-2x+6$, so $y=-\dfrac{2}{3}x+2$ and $m=-\dfrac{2}{3}$.
$\tan\theta=-\dfrac{2}{3}$
The calculator returns a negative angle. Add $180^{\circ}$ before rounding:
$\theta=\tan^{-1}\left(-\dfrac{2}{3}\right)+180^{\circ}$
$\approx146^{\circ}$
